I have my own sort of pet issue with economics and I am frustrated to never hear it discussed. It’s basically that a dollar is essentially one share of the stock of the net value of all goods traded in dollars.

So if you take all the goods traded in dollars and divide them by the number of dollars in circulation, that ought to set the value.

So if you increase the amount of goods without increasing the number of dollars, it increases the value of a dollar. However, we give this the scary name of “deflation.”

But you want that.. either way, even if you do increase the number of dollars, you still want more goods, because they’re the actual wealth that the money is just a representation of.

And physical, manufactured or harvested goods and resources are the closest to that premise. In order, extraction and production are most critical, then logistics, then after that, service sector shit. The further you get from manufacturing raw goods and performing value added processes, the more justification is required for that area to be your focus.

So our economic priorities are totally upside down.

That was actually almost what used to be the case when we had commodity money, such as with the gold standard from the late XIX century until the end of the Bretton Woods agreements (the so-called “Nixon shock”). With fiat money, this isn't the case, since fiat money is not expressibly convertible to anything else: it only has value insofar as others give it. This makes the value of fiat money much more volatile, more susceptible to financial operations independent from the service and physical goods trade market.

Mind you, I'm not trying to make an argument here on whether fiat money is better or worse than commodity money, both have upsides and downsides. The key point in reply to your comment, though, is that no, with fiat money it's not true that limiting the amount of currency increases its value.

Concerning deflation, moreover, the situation is even more complicated, and that's true regardless of what kind of currency you're using: the effects of limitations on circulating money are extremely non-linear, due to the large impact this has on the amount of trade, and thus affects the so-called “velocity of money” —and trade stagnation is not a good thing. It's a bit like the human circulatory system. Very high pulse rate is bad (=> hyperinflation), but very low pulse rate is bad too: if your heart stops, and blood doesn't circulate, you're dead. And finding the proper balance isn't trivial.
